# Ray Tracing {#sec-ray-tracing}

::: {.callout-tip title="Related Chapters"}
For cold-plasma dispersion relations and refractive indices, see @sec-waves and @sec-CPDR; for WKB/geometrical optics foundations, see @sec-WKB; for kinetic dispersion solvers, see @sec-dispersion.
:::

Wave heating is one of the most important approaches to heating a plasma to high temperature. In magnetically confined plasmas, the waves commonly used from high frequency ($\sim 100\ \mathrm{GHz}$) to low frequency ($<1\ \mathrm{MHz}$) include the electron cyclotron wave (ECW, or whistler wave), lower hybrid wave (LHW), ion cyclotron wave (ICW), and Alfvén wave (AW). There are also terminologies such as fast wave (FW), slow wave (SW), helicon wave, etc. A simple yet accurate way to study wave propagation and heating is using the _geometrical optics (WKB) approximation_ (@sec-WKB), which yields the _ray tracing equations_.

## Background

In optics, the refractive index is a measure of how much a material bends or refracts light as it passes through it. It is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to the phase speed of light in the material:
$$
n = \frac{c}{v_\mathrm{ph}}
$$
where $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum, and $v_\mathrm{ph}$ is the phase speed of the wave in the material.

In a plasma, the refractive index depends on the plasma parameters, such as the density, temperature, and magnetic field (see @sec-CPDR for the full magnetized cold-plasma dispersion relation). For an unmagnetized collisional plasma, the squared refractive index is given by:
$$
n^2 = 1 - \frac{\omega_p^2}{\omega(\omega + i\nu_{en})}
$$ {#eq-plasma-refractive-index}
where $\omega_p$ is the plasma frequency (@eq-plasma_frequency), $\nu_{en}$ is the electron-neutral collision frequency, $\omega$ is the frequency of the incident wave, and $i$ is the imaginary unit. In a magnetized plasma, the electron cyclotron frequency $\omega_{ce}=eB/m_e$ and propagation angle enter via the Appleton–Hartree / cold-plasma dispersion tensor (@sec-CPDR). The plasma refractive index can be complex, meaning that it has both real and imaginary parts:

* The real part of the refractive index determines the phase speed of the wave in the plasma, while
* The imaginary part determines the attenuation or absorption of the wave as it passes through the plasma.

The refractive index plays an important role in determining the behavior of electromagnetic waves in plasmas, and is therefore a key parameter in plasma ray tracing simulations.

## How It Works

In plasma ray tracing, the refractive index of the plasma is calculated based on the plasma parameters, such as the density, temperature, and magnetic field, and the ray is traced through the plasma using Snell's law at interfaces:
$$
n_1 \sin(\theta_1) = n_2 \sin(\theta_2)
$$ {#eq-snell-law}
where $n_1$ and $n_2$ are the refractive indices of the media on either side of the interface, $\theta_1$ is the angle of incidence, and $\theta_2$ is the angle of refraction. This allows us to study how waves interact with plasma and how they can be used to probe and manipulate the properties of the plasma.

In Hamiltonian form, the ray tracing equations in Cartesian coordinates are
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \mathbf{k}} = -\frac{\partial D/\partial \mathbf{k}}{\partial D/\partial \omega} = \mathbf{v}_g \\
\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{k}}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -\frac{\partial \omega}{\partial \mathbf{r}} = \frac{\partial D/\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial D/\partial \omega}
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ray-tracing}
with the local dispersion relation
$$
D(\omega,\mathbf{k},\mathbf{r}) = 0
$$
where $\mathbf{r}=(x,y,z)$ is the spatial location, $\mathbf{k}=(k_x, k_y, k_z)$ is the wave vector, $\omega$ is the wave frequency, and $\mathbf{v}_g$ is the group velocity.

::: {.callout-warning title="Validity of Geometrical Optics"}
The geometrical optics approximation is valid when _the wavelength is much smaller than the background inhomogeneity scale length_ ($\lambda \ll L$). This is usually well satisfied for high-frequency waves such as ECW and LHW, but must be used with caution for low-frequency waves such as ICW and Alfvén waves.
:::

For a more thorough introduction, check out [@tracy2014ray].
